4.1.crux: Metals are usually shiny, hard, can be beaten into sheets and drawn into wires, ring when struck and conduct heat and electricity; non-metals usually don't.

cards.title: Metal or non-metal?
say: Iron, copper, aluminium, gold and silver are metals.
Sulphur, carbon (coal), oxygen and phosphorus are non-metals.

cards.title: Metals in action

items.sub: School bells are made of metal

say: We use each property of metals in daily life.

cards.title: Surprises

items.sub: Metals so soft they can be cut with a knife

say: Most metals are hard, but a few are soft.
Most non-metals don't conduct electricity, but graphite does.
cards.remember: Rules have exceptions: sodium is a soft metal, graphite is a conducting non-metal.

crux_points: Metals: shiny, malleable, ductile, sonorous, good conductors.
Non-metals: dull, brittle, not sonorous, poor conductors.
There are exceptions, like soft sodium and conducting graphite.

quiz.q: Aluminium can be beaten into thin foil. This property is called…
quiz.why: Malleable materials can be beaten into thin sheets.

quiz.q: Coal breaks into pieces when hammered. Coal is…
quiz.why: Non-metals like coal are brittle: they break instead of flattening.

4.2.crux: Metals form basic oxides and give hydrogen with acids; non-metals form acidic oxides; a more reactive metal pushes a less reactive one out of its compound.

cards.title: Burning in oxygen
say: Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides, which are basic.
Non-metals react with oxygen to form oxides, which are acidic.
cards.remember: Metal oxide = basic; non-metal oxide = acidic.

cards.title: Rusting
say: Iron left in moist air gets a brown, flaky coat called rust (iron oxide).
Copper in moist air gets a dull green coating instead.

cards.title: With water and acids

items.sub: Reacts so fast it's kept in kerosene
Catches fire, so it's kept in water
Gives hydrogen gas: 'pop' with a burning match

say: Some metals and non-metals are so reactive they must be stored carefully.
Hydrogen gas burns with a pop sound.

cards.title: Displacement
say: Iron is more reactive than copper, so it pushes copper out of copper sulphate.
Iron + copper sulphate → iron sulphate + copper.
cards.remember: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one. Copper can't displace iron or zinc.

crux_points: Metals form basic oxides; non-metals form acidic oxides.
Metals react with acids to give hydrogen; non-metals usually don't.
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound.

quiz.q: An iron nail is left in blue copper sulphate. What happens?
options: The solution turns green and copper coats the nail
quiz.why: Iron displaces copper: iron sulphate (green) forms and brown copper coats the nail.

quiz.q: The oxide of sulphur dissolved in water turns blue litmus…
quiz.why: Non-metal oxides make acids, which turn blue litmus red.

quiz.q: Why is sodium stored in kerosene?
options: It reacts strongly with air and water
quiz.why: Sodium reacts vigorously with oxygen and water, so it is kept in kerosene.

4.3.crux: We choose metals and non-metals for jobs that match their properties, from copper wires to oxygen for breathing.

cards.title: Uses of metals
say: Each use matches a property: copper conducts electricity, so it's used in wires.

cards.title: Uses of non-metals

items.name: Oxygen
items.eg: Needed by all living things to breathe

say: Non-metals are just as important as metals in our lives.

cards.title: Match the property to the use
say: Look around your home: can you guess why each object is made of its material?

crux_points: Metals are used for machines, vehicles, wires, utensils and jewellery.
Non-metals give us oxygen to breathe, fertilisers, water treatment and antiseptics.
Every use matches a property of the material.

quiz.q: Why are electric wires made of copper?
options: Copper is ductile and a good conductor
quiz.why: Copper can be drawn into wires and conducts electricity very well.

quiz.q: Which non-metal is used to purify drinking water?
quiz.why: Chlorine kills germs in drinking water.
